newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Botswana proposes emerging nations business forum.
newsitem.headline: Botswana proposes emerging nations business forum.

text.p: Botswana President Sir Ketumile Masire on Tuesday proposed the establishment of an emerging nations business forum for Southern Africa and round tables to bring together governments and their private sectors.

"This would create the environment for promoting southern Africa as a growth area," Masire told a news conference at the close of a business conference hosted by his country which was attended by 14 African nations.
He said he wanted to explore the setting up of a regional Southern Africa Business Advisory Group, and added:
"There would be national action groups in the individual participating countries with members from the government, the private sector and the workforce."
Business councils in each country would monitor implementation and progress.
Masire said southern Africa would have to promote joint investment so that roads, railways, power and water could be organised on a regional and cooperative basis.

The conference was called to debate "Smart Partnerships." Conceived in Malaysia, it is a philosophy of promoting "cooperative competitiveness" based on the premise that governments, the private sector and individuals must work together for long-term mutual gains.

Presidents Bakili Muluzi of Malawi, Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe, Sam Nujoma of Namibia, Jerry Rawlings of Ghana, Joaquim Chissano of Mozambique, Benjamim Mkapa of Tanzania and Yoweri Museveni of Uganda all attended.
President Nelson Mandela of South Africa, prevented from attending earlier because of his involvement in the Zairean peace talks, joined the conference for the closing session.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Bin Mahamad was a special guest at the conference, which he rated "very successful."
"What is the use of independence if there is no economic independence?" Mahathir told reporters at a briefing. "Now is the time to make independence meaningful to the ordinary people."

Earlier in the week, the Malaysian leader attacked Western financial institutions for "corrupting" Africa with aid and for promoting development programmes that served to enrich the nations of the developing world.
